'''Mike Shrine''' (御食神社, *Mike-jinja*) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|qid=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} that serves as a subordinate shrine (摂社) of {{ill|Toyōke Daijingū|ja|豊受大神宮}} (the Outer Shrine) of {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|en|Ise Shrine|qid=Q687168|lt=Ise Grand Shrine}}. It is Ranked 15th among the 16 subordinate shrines of the Outer Shrine.<ref>Ujiyamada City Hall (1929): pp. 11–13.</ref>
Locally, it is revered as a {{ill|Ubusunagami|en|Ubusunagami|qid=Q1392097|lt=Ubusunagami}} (guardian deity of one's birthplace) and affectionately called "Tatsukami-san." <ref name="ic7">Ise Culture Publishing (2008): p. 47.</ref>

maritime gateway to Ise.<ref name="ic67">Ise Bunka Publishing (2008): pp.46-47</ref> The precincts are surrounded by a pond and moat, believed to be remnants of a former inlet connected to the sea.<ref name="gk">Gakken Publishing (2013): p.63</ref><ref name="eg">Furukawa Ken, "[https://web.archive.org/web/20131213130254/http://www.geocities.jp/engisiki/ise/bun/is080123-01.html Mikenojinja Shrine]" (accessed September 29, 2013)</ref>
The enshrined deity is {{ill|Minato no Miketsukami|ja|水戸御饗都神}}, the god of sacred offerings (御饌) made from marine products landed at Kamiya-shiro Port for {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|en|Ise Shrine|qid=Q687168|lt=Ise Grand Shrine}}.<ref name="ic7"/> "Minato" refers to a port where seawater reaches inland.<ref name="gk"/>
The shrine building is enclosed by a single tamagaki (sacred fence) and has no saisenbako (offertory box). In front of the main hall stands a chozubachi (water basin) shaped like a boat.<ref name="ic7"/> A well called "Tatsu no I" within the precincts is revered as a fire prevention talisman.<ref name="ic6">Ise Bunka Publishing (2008): pp.46-47</ref> The local festival group is known as the "Tatsu-gumi."<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.isekanko.jp/k-cycling/course03.html|title=Course 03: Boat Pilgrimage Route|publisher=Ise City Tourism Association|accessdate=2013-09-29|archiveurl=https://megalodon.jp/2013-0929-1615-48/www.isekanko.jp/k-cycling/course03.html|archivedate=2013-09-29}}</ref>
== History ==
The shrine traces its origins to the "Miketsu Jinja" (水饗神社) mentioned in the *Yamato-hime-no-mikoto Seiki*.<ref name="ic7"/> It was founded to honor the service of WASHITORI no Okina, who presented pure water to {{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto|en|Yamatohime-no-mikoto|qid=Q4388732|lt=Yamatohime-no-mikoto}}. The "Tatsu no I" well in the precincts is said to be the very source from which the water was drawn.<ref name="ic7"/>
Mikenojinja was certainly established before 927 CE (Enchō 5), as it appears in the *Engishiki Jinmyōchō*.<ref>Ise Bunka Publishing (2008): p.22</ref> It also appears in the *Toyukemiya Gishikichō*, suggesting it existed before 804 CE (Enryaku 23).<ref name="sk8">Shikinaisha Kenkyūkai (1990): p.258</ref>
In the early modern period, after a period of neglect, the shrine was restored at its current location in 1663 (Kanbun 3).<ref name="sk7">Shikinaisha Kenkyūkai (1990): p.257</ref>
== Festivals ==
The "Water Drawing" ceremony (お水取り) is held annually on the first {{ill|Day of the Dragon|ja|辰の日}} of the New Year.<ref name="km">{{Cite web|url=http://www.kankomie.or.jp/event/detail_15247.html|title=Annual Water Drawing Ceremony at Mikenojinja|publisher=Mie Prefecture Tourism Federation|accessdate=2013-09-29|archiveurl=https://megalodon.jp/2013-0929-1017-39/www.kankomie.or.jp/event/detail_15247.html|archivedate=2013-09-29}}</ref> Water drawn from the "Tatsu no I" well is distributed to worshippers, believed to offer protection against fire and water disasters for the year.<ref name="ic6"/>
During the {{ill|Oshiraishimochi|ja|お白石持|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q17225061}} ritual, water from the well is sprinkled along the path as white stones are carried to the shrine.<ref>Ise Bunka Publishing (2013): p.7</ref>
== Access ==
Mikenojinja is located in the historic Kamiya-shiro Port district.
* **By Bus:** Approx. 3 minutes on foot from the "Kamiya-shiro Port" bus stop served by Mie Kotsu.
* **By Car:** About 2 minutes (1.4 km) from the "Ogicho 1" intersection on National Route 23 via Mie Prefectural Route 201. No dedicated parking is available.
